question: In Mosquitto 2.x, the allow_anonymous parameter is specified BEFORE the first listener. How is it applied?

options.text: Causes a configuration error in Mosquitto 2.x
options.explanation: There's no error — this is valid syntax. The global allow_anonymous works as a default for all listeners.

options.text: Ignored in Mosquitto 2.x — must be specified inside listener
options.explanation: It's not ignored — it's applied as a default. But best practice is to explicitly specify allow_anonymous inside each listener for readability and config predictability.

options.text: Applied to all listeners as the default value
options.explanation: In Mosquitto 2.x, security parameters before the first listener become global defaults for all listeners. Each listener can override this value with its own allow_anonymous.

options.text: Applied only to the first listener
options.explanation: The parameter before the first listener is a global default for ALL listeners. If you need different behavior, specify allow_anonymous inside each listener block.

question: What changed in the configuration syntax when migrating from Mosquitto 1.x to 2.x?

options.text: allow_anonymous is now false by default (was true)
options.explanation: Breaking change in v2.0: anonymous access is denied by default. v1.x configs without explicit allow_anonymous stop working after the update.

options.text: port and bind_address parameters now work only inside a listener block
options.explanation: In v1.x, port and bind_address were global. In v2.x, they became part of listener syntax: listener 1883 192.168.1.1 (port and address on one line).

options.text: TLS parameters (cafile, certfile, keyfile) are now specified inside listener
options.explanation: In v1.x, TLS parameters could be global. In v2.x, they must be inside a specific listener — logical since different listeners can have different certificates.

options.text: Password file format changed to JSON
options.explanation: The password file format remains the same (username:hashed_password). The hashing algorithm changed (PBKDF2-SHA512 instead of SHA1), but not the file format.

question: Which log_dest is recommended for OpenWRT and why?

options.text: syslog — integrates with system journal, readable via logread
options.explanation: syslog is the standard logging mechanism for OpenWRT. Logs are available via logread, don't require a separate file, and are automatically rotated by the system. Ideal for embedded devices.

options.text: topic — publish logs to $SYS/broker/log for monitoring
options.explanation: Publishing logs to a topic creates recursive load: each log query generates an MQTT message, which itself generates a log. For monitoring, use $SYS topics directly.

options.text: stdout — convenient for seeing logs in real time
options.explanation: stdout is useful for manual debugging runs. In production, the service is launched via init.d and stdout is lost. For continuous operation — syslog.

options.text: file /var/log/mosquitto.log — standard Linux log path
options.explanation: /var/log/ in OpenWRT is stored on flash. Continuous log writing wears out flash memory. If you need file logging, use /tmp/mosquitto.log (tmpfs).

question:
The config has: listener 1883
allow_anonymous false
password_file /etc/mosquitto/passwd
listener 9001
protocol websockets. Does the WebSocket listener require authentication?

options.text: Yes — allow_anonymous false acts globally for the entire process
options.explanation: In Mosquitto 2.x, allow_anonymous is a per-listener setting. To apply to all listeners, either specify it globally BEFORE the first listener or repeat it in each one.

options.text: No — allow_anonymous and password_file apply only to the first listener
options.explanation: In Mosquitto 2.x, authentication parameters belong to the listener under which they are listed. The second listener (9001) has no own authentication settings — you must explicitly add allow_anonymous and password_file under it.

options.text: The config is invalid — two listeners can't have different settings
options.explanation: Two listeners with different settings is an absolutely valid configuration and common practice. For example: a local listener without passwords + an external one with authentication.

options.text: Yes — authentication parameters apply to all listeners after them
options.explanation: No, parameters apply only to the listener under which they are listed. Each listener is independent. If you need authentication on port 9001, add the parameters explicitly.

question: The command kill -HUP $(cat /var/run/mosquitto.pid) is executed after changing mosquitto.conf. What will NOT be applied?

options.text: Changing the listener port (e.g., from 1883 to 1884)
options.explanation: Listener parameters are network sockets already opened. SIGHUP cannot close the old port and open a new one without a restart. To change the port, use /etc/init.d/mosquitto restart.

options.text: Enabling persistence (persistence false → true)
options.explanation: Persistence parameters require a restart — the broker cannot 'on the fly' open a database for already running connections. You need /etc/init.d/mosquitto restart.

options.text: Adding a new user to password_file
options.explanation: password_file is re-read on SIGHUP. If you add a user via mosquitto_passwd and send HUP, the new user can connect without a restart.

options.text: Changing log_type from notice to debug
options.explanation: Logging parameters (log_type, log_dest) are applied on SIGHUP without a restart. This is convenient for temporarily enabling debug logs on a running system.

question: What is the default value of max_connections in Mosquitto?

options.text: 0 (all connections prohibited until explicitly allowed)
options.explanation: 0 would mean a complete ban, which makes no sense. The default is -1 — unlimited. A value of 0 would immediately reject all clients.

options.text: 1000 connections
options.explanation: 1000 is not the default. The default is -1 (no limit). Mosquitto is designed for scaling — some production installations handle hundreds of thousands of connections.

options.text: -1 (no limit)
options.explanation: By default, max_connections = -1, meaning no limit. The broker accepts as many connections as the system resources allow. On a router, it's recommended to set an explicit limit.

options.text: 100 connections
options.explanation: 100 is not the default. The default value is -1. For OpenWRT with 128 MB RAM, a reasonable limit is 50-200, but this needs to be set explicitly.
